name: Elena Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Elena. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for my uncle Gareth's building firm, Evans and Sons, even though there's no sons left in it, just me and three men. We do extensions, loft conversions and roofs around our market town. Today I was on a kitchen extension on Chapel Row, cutting rafters with Gareth watching over my shoulder. I'm still the slowest on the team and I measure everything three times, but he says that's better than the other way round.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come into the trade?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I left school at sixteen because I couldn't stand the classroom, and Gareth said he'd take me on if I turned up every day at half seven. I've not missed a day in nine years. Nobody else in the family wanted it, and I didn't want the firm to close when he retires. I still live at home with Mum and Dad, so most of my pay goes straight into the savings for when Tom and I marry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and leave it at that. I don't go online much, I'm not on any of the apps. After church I'd probably say to Tom's dad that the computers came to nothing, and he'd agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd be a relief. I've never used one of those AI things and I never want to. People round here want a builder they know, someone whose family they've known for years. If AI comes to nothing, the firm stays the same, and that's what I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on exactly as I am. Keep turning up, keep learning to cut a roof properly, and keep saving. I've got over a year's pay put by, and Tom's family have said we can build on a corner of their land. We'd marry next summer, at St Mary's, like we planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled. It's the life I'd choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Gareth's firm mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grandad started Evans and Sons after the war with a handcart, and I want to be the one keeping it going. When Gareth retires I'll take it on, even if I have to hire a proper roofer to do the bits I can't. That matters more to me than any wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at all you'd worry about in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only Gareth's health. He's sixty-one and his back is bad, and if he stopped tomorrow I'm not ready to run it. But that's nothing to do with computers. That's just life.

After church I'd tell Tom's dad the **computers** came to nothing.

do: Keep turning up and learning to **cut a roof** properly.
Keep saving from **over a year's** pay already put by.
Marry Tom next summer at **St Mary's** and plan a house on his family's land.
feel: **Calm** and **settled**, living the life she'd choose.

fieldNote: Her loyalty is to the **family firm** more than the wage.

Keep saving most of her pay while living at home
Marry Tom next summer at St Mary's as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office people's worry, not ours. Round here people still want a real builder in their kitchen. I wouldn't make a fuss about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I don't think it touches me much. Gareth does the quotes on paper at the kitchen table, and maybe the bigger firms would start doing theirs with computers. But nobody's sending a robot up a ladder on Chapel Row any time soon, and my hands are what I'm paid for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, honestly. I'd keep saving and keep learning roofs. If Gareth wanted to try one of those quoting programs, that would be his choice, not mine. I'd wait and see what the big firms do with it before I worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Maybe a bit curious what the big firms get up to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the bigger firms start quoting cheaper because of the AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then some people would go with them, the ones who always want the cheapest. But our customers are mostly people who've used us for thirty years, or their kids, and that's not something a computer gets you. Gareth fitted Mrs Pugh's kitchen in 1998 and she's just had us back for her loft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Bethan, who works in the council planning office. If AI takes over checking and writing, that's her whole job. She's got two little ones and a mortgage. I'd pray for her, and I'd tell her she can always come and carry timber for us.

say: It's the **office people's** worry, not ours.
People round here still want a **real builder** in their kitchen.
think: Gareth does quotes **on paper**, and only big firms would use **computers**.
Nobody's sending a **robot up a ladder** here soon, and my hands earn my pay.
do: Keep **saving** and learning roofs as now.
Leave any **quoting program** to Gareth and wait to see what big firms do.
feel: Mostly **calm**, a bit **curious** about the big firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a terrible thing to rush on people, and that families and churches will have to look after each other, because the government won't manage it. I wouldn't be online about it, but I'd say it at the Sunday lunch table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's bad for the firm. In 2028 the big builders would get AI doing their quotes and planning for nothing, and they'd undercut Gareth. They'd have robots that can do extensions three years later. By 2031 I'd be thirty-one, trying to keep my grandad's building firm alive against machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save even harder and stop spending on anything but the wedding. Tom and I would probably build a smaller house than we'd planned, so we don't owe much. I'd lean on Tom's family, the farm will always need hands, and I'd ask Gareth what he wants to do with the firm. I still wouldn't touch the AI, I'd rather build things than type.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got money and family, but I can see the firm going under.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Three years between the AI and the robots. What would you do with that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do as much work as we can while people still want us, and pay off anything we owe. Gareth would probably want to retire then rather than fight it. I'd have to decide whether to try to keep Evans and Sons going on my own. Honestly, I don't know if I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tom say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom would say the farm will feed us whatever happens, and he's probably right. His dad says the same about the machines on the farm, that they still need someone who knows the land. I'd be working on the farm in a pinch, and I'd hate it, but I'd do it.

say: It's terrible to **rush** this on people, so **families and churches** must help each other.
I'd say it at the **Sunday lunch** table, not online.
think: Big builders with AI quotes in **2028** would **undercut** Gareth.
By **2031** I'd be fighting machines to keep my **grandad's firm** alive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time enough for people to prepare, and that families should sort themselves out rather than wait for the government. I'd say we need more apprenticeships, not fewer, so young people know how to do things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years plus three gets the robots to 2034. I'd have learned roofs properly by then, and Gareth would be about ready to retire anyway. It feels like enough time to have a family and run the firm a few years. But I'd still wonder what's left for Evans and Sons after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, marry Tom next summer and build the house as we planned. I'd keep saving and learn the money side of the firm from Gareth, the quotes and the books, while he's still here. I wouldn't learn the computer stuff, but I'd let Tom's sister Ffion do our quotes on it if she wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more at peace than the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd learn the books but not the AI. Isn't the AI going to do the books?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for the big firms. But somebody has to know what a fair price is for Mrs Pugh's loft, and that's Gareth's head, not a machine. I'd want that in my head too. If Ffion wants to put it in the computer after, that's her business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children, if you had them, about the trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children to learn a trade with their hands, the way I did, whatever the robots are doing. Hands that can fix a roof are never wasted, even if it's only your own roof. And they'd learn to turn up at half seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and people should stop fretting and get on with their lives. Keep the apprenticeships going and look after your own. That's what I'd say at church and at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, with robots around 2039 I'd be forty and probably running the firm by then. Gareth would be long retired. That's a long time, and a lot can happen. I'd hope the people round here still want a builder they know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as always: marry Tom, build the house, keep learning, and take over from Gareth when he's ready, probably around 2031. I'd put some of my savings into the firm, a new van and proper roofing kit. I wouldn't bother with the AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It's too far off to fret about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Putting your savings into the firm sounds like a big step. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's my grandad's name and I'll be the one carrying it. A new van with Evans and Sons on the side says the family firm is not going anywhere. If the robots come in 2039, I'll deal with it then, but I'm not going to let the firm look tired before they do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you hire anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An apprentice, definitely, a local lad or lass who's not suited to school, like I was. Gareth gave me a chance and I'd want to give someone else one. That's how it's always worked here.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the firm would be undercut before I'd had a chance to run it. What would help is the government getting out of the way of small builders, cutting the paperwork, and keeping apprenticeships funded, so firms like ours can keep going and keep training people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. Whatever happens with the machines, we've got the church and the families round here, and people look after each other. That's worth more than any computer.

headlineQuote: Whatever happens with the machines, we've got the church and the families round here, and people look after each other.
portrait: Elena is a **27-year-old junior builder** in her uncle's small family firm, slow but careful.
She lives at home, has **over a year** of pay saved and plans to marry **Tom**, a farmer's son.
She has **never used AI** and trusts local reputation, faith and family over technology.
Her real fear is big firms **undercutting** her grandad's firm with AI quotes, then robots.
She is **calm** most of the time, **anxious** only when AGI comes by 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with the family firm **undercut** before she can run it.
whatWouldHelp: Less **paperwork** for small builders and funded **apprenticeships**.
